strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem: accelerating Sinkhorn through learned initializations while retaining subsequent solver refinement. Predicting unregularized dual potentials and applying a C-transform is a well-motivated construction.

Adversarial generation of synthetic training pairs is a potentially useful contribution beyond dataset-specific learned initializers, allowing training without samples from the eventual application dataset.

The experiments show consistent improvements over uniform initialization across four datasets. Tables 1–2 support average iteration reductions of approximately 16% and 33% at marginal-error tolerances of 1e-3 and 1e-2, respectively. Reporting marginal feasibility and runtime alongside transport-cost error strengthens this evidence.
The architecture, training pseudocode, principal hyperparameters, and code link facilitate understanding and reproduction. Proposition 7 provides a valid, though limited, objective-value bound.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish competitiveness with existing initialization methods. The downstream experiments compare only against uniform initialization, omitting the cited Thornton–Cuturi approaches. Figure 3 evaluates the Amos et al. loss only through potential MSE, which is sensitive to gauge and does not necessarily predict Sinkhorn convergence. Comparisons using runtime to matched marginal tolerances are needed.

The distinctive adversarial training component is not isolated experimentally. There is no comparison against the same supervised approximator trained with a fixed generator or simple random sampling under a matched labeling budget. Consequently, the observed improvements cannot be attributed to adversarial sample generation, leaving the principal methodological contribution insufficiently supported.

The claim of generalization to any pair of distributions of fixed dimension substantially exceeds the evidence. All experiments use one 28×28 grid, one cost matrix, one regularization value, and four selected data sources. These results support transfer across the tested datasets, but not arbitrary distributions even within that fixed dimension. Concentrated or strongly shifted distributions and a regularization sweep would provide more convincing coverage.

Section 3.3 interprets Proposition 7 too strongly: an entropic dual objective gap does not establish closeness of potentials, scaling vectors, or improved iteration complexity. Dual potentials can be nonunique beyond their additive gauge. Moreover, the bound mnε is approximately 153.7 in the experiments, whereas individual transport costs are at most 2, making it uninformative at the evaluated setting.

The standalone barycenter claim is supported only by four qualitative images, without reference barycenters, objective errors, or accuracy–runtime comparisons. The proposed error-cancellation explanation assumes unbiased prediction errors without evidence; unbiased scalar estimates would also not establish reliable optimization. The handling of simplex constraints and differentiation through predicted potentials needs clarification.

Several experimental details remain unspecified: test-pair counts, repeated training runs, confidence-interval construction, the test preprocessing offset, and numerical precision or stabilization at the very small regularization value. These omissions limit assessment of robustness and reproduction of the reported speedups. Together with the missing baselines and ablations, they make rejection more appropriate despite the promising gains.
